To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
short alleles of both GGCN and CAG repeats are associated to increased AR and PSA staining, and with more advanced Gleason scores in human prostatic cancers.

short alleles of CAG repeats at exon 1 of androgen receptor gene (AR) are associated to increased prostate-specific antigen (PSA) staining and higher Gleason score, and that short alleles of both CAG and GGG repeats at AR gene are associated with more aggressive forms (Gleason score of 8 or higher) of prostate cancer.
short alleles at both GGN and the CAG repeats of the AR exon 1 are associated to increased AR staining, PSA staining, and to higher Gleason score.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular mechanisms of the human prostate cancer development, with the aim of finding new markers of aggressivity and prognosis.
a genetic polymorphism of the human AR gene, the CAG and GNN tracts, and their relationship to the AR protein and PSA immunohistochemical staining in prostate cancer.
the study of the androgenic signalling in prostate cancer and its relation to the genetic variability of the androgen-receptor gene.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the shorter alleles at both tracts of the AR gene are not only a risk factor for CaP, but also for more aggressive forms of CaP.
the combination of short alleles for both CAG and GNN polymorphisms in the AR exon 1, is significantly associated to increased AR signalling intensity and to more aggressive prostate cancer.
shorter alleles at both the GGN and the CAG repeats of the AR gene are more common in the most aggressive forms of prostate cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
short alleles of both CAG and GAG repeats at the AR gene are markers of more aggressive forms of CaP.
shorter GGN repeats are associated with a more aggressive form of the disease, as shown by a higher PSA score and Gleason score.

shorter alleles of the CAG and GGG repeats at the AR gene are related to more aggressive forms of human prostate cancer, probably by increasing the AR signalling intensity, as suggested by "in vitro" studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the AR protein staining is positively associated with the Gleason grade in human prostate cancer.
the shorter GGN repeats are associated to increased AR protein expression and to more aggressive forms of human prostate cancer.
the combination of short alleles of the CAG and GNN repeats of the AR gene may be a useful biomarker of the aggressiveness of prostate cancer.
